title: The hand writes (Avot 3:16)
hookLine: Akiva: the shop is open, the ledger is open, and the hand writes
tomorrow: can anyone learn on an empty stomach? one rabbi says no.

cards: Somebody hits record at rehearsal, and suddenly everyone stands up straighter. A camera does that. Akiva lived without one, and still he pictured a record of every day: a shop that never closes.
The shop is open, the shopkeeper gives credit, the ledger is open, and the hand writes.

teach.b: The whole saying in Avot is a picture of life as a store. Everything is given on pledge, Akiva says, and a net is spread over all the living. Whoever wants to borrow may come and borrow.
Notice who may borrow: whoever wants to. Nobody is turned away at the door. Collectors make their rounds every day, and they take payment with a person's knowledge or without.
It can sound like a security camera. But follow it to the end. The judgment is a judgment of truth, he says, and everything is prepared for the feast.
So the ledger isn't there to catch you. It's there because what you do is real enough to write down.
You've been trusted with credit: a life, a body, a day.
And the book ends at a table.
This week, that's the gift. Not fear of being watched, but the plain fact that the small things count, the ones no camera catches, and the ledger is still open.

how: Avot 3:16's ledger image runs through Jewish thought about the High Holy Days, when the prayers speak of books opened and deeds recorded; here Akiva uses it for every day.

o: every deed is written in an open ledger
a signature sealing a business contract
a scribe copying out a Torah scroll

s: his last words: everything is prepared for the feast.
in Akiva's picture, the shopkeeper gives credit
the shop is open, and whoever wants to borrow may borrow.
only deeds someone sees get written down
collectors take payment with a person's knowledge or without.

games.q: you're alone at work late. a coworker's mistake would be easy to pin on them, and no one would ever find out. Akiva's shop says:
o: the hand writes either way; act as if it's in the ledger.
no camera, no record, so it doesn't really count.
only big deeds are written; small ones don't matter.
games.why: collectors come with a person's knowledge or without. Akiva's ledger records what no camera sees.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. In your own hand, write one line about something you did yesterday that you'd be glad to see in the ledger, and one line for what you'd like the hand to write today.
Keep the paper where you'll find it.

wordCard.voice: The hand writes. Akiva's ledger, the pinkas: life given on credit, every deed written, and the book ending at a feast.

orig.note: Hebrew: and the hand writes, from Akiva's shop parable.

carryVoice: The line for today: the hand writes, and the book ends in a feast. Be well.
